transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-11-18
Time: 16:00 UTC (09:00 PT)
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Alex Kim (Redwood AE), Sara Patel (Redwood SE), Jordan Lee (Atlas), Priya Rao (Atlas), Marcus Nguyen (Atlas)
---
00:00 Alex Kim: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick intros 
 - i'm alex, i'm the AE on this account, sara is our solutions engineer who will do the console walkthrough. how's everyone doing?
00:08 Jordan Lee: good thanks, excited to see the tracing stuff. we run a pretty bursty inference workload, mostly on dedicated gpus but we are evaluating hosted for dev.
00:16 Priya Rao: hi all, i'm priya, head of platform. main goal is observability and fast debugging 
 - sometimes our teams spend days tracking down model regressions.
00:24 Marcus Nguyen: security manager here, will focus on compliance, audit logs, encryption at rest and in transit.
00:30 Sara Patel: awesome, i'll share my screen in a sec, we'll go through tracing, error analysis, request logs and typical debugging flows. i'll also point out RBAC and data residency controls.
00:38 Alex Kim: quick agenda 
 - console walkthrough, demo of trace-to-log flow, how to pivot from a failed response to a request log and the KV cache traces, then Q&A and next steps.
00:50 Sara Patel: (shares screen) ok starting on the dashboard, this is per-route latency breakdown, token counts, and a tracing tab on the left. note: some of the names in the UI are shorthand; the tracers map to internal span ids, sometimes they'll appear as ervice instead of service in the auto transcript, sorry for that.
01:05 Jordan Lee: can you show an example of a low-latency outlier and how we'd debug it?
01:12 Sara Patel: sure 
 - here's a trace of a request that spiked to 2.1s. at the top you see model selection, runtime queue, kernel selection spans. you can click into the runtime queue span to see queue wait ms and batching size. we also show kv cache hits/misses 
 - in this case the kv cache miss rate was high because prefix caching didn't apply.
01:32 Jordan Lee: kv cache is our main concern; our sessions are long and we use prefix caching heavily. any suggestions?
01:38 Sara Patel: yep 
 - console suggests adding prefix keys for stable prompts, and you can toggle quantization variants per model in the model catalog tab. for long sessions, enabling persistent KV caching on dedicated instances reduces tail latency.
01:50 Marcus Nguyen: how do we see which user triggered the request? we need user-level audit logs for compliance.
01:56 Sara Patel: good question 
 - request logs include tokenized prompt length, request_id, and metadata fields. if you send an identity header or session id it will be attached to the request log. audit logs are retained per account and can be forwarded to your SIEM via our S3 export or syslog connector (we'll share the doc link).
02:10 Alex Kim: small note, the SSO/SCIM integration maps Redwood users to RBAC roles so you can restrict access to tracing views.
02:18 Priya Rao: what's the retention for tracing vs raw request logs?
02:22 Sara Patel: tracing typically retained 30 days by default, request logs configurable up to 13 months for enterprise accounts. long-term retention is an add-on.
02:30 Jordan Lee: what about PII in logs, do we mask prompts?
02:34 Sara Patel: we support configurable masking and prompt redaction at ingestion; you can also opt for no storage if you want ephemeral logs for HIPAA-sensitive flows. we'll include the KMS/HSM options in the security docs.
02:46 Marcus Nguyen: good. about KMS 
 - customer-managed keys or do you use a Redwood-managed key?
02:50 Alex Kim: both options. for Private deployments we support customer KMS/HSM. in hosted you can bring-your-own-key with AWS KMS integration.
02:58 Jordan Lee: let's talk about error analysis 
 - how do you group errors across models/versions?
03:05 Sara Patel: console error analysis groups by error class and upstream cause; you can pivot from an error group to sample request logs, and to span-level stack traces for the runtime. there's a rate chart and a sample set; the sampling is adjustable 
 - we show head and tail samples.
03:20 Priya Rao: do you support regression alerting based on prompt sets?
03:24 Sara Patel: yes 
 - Optimize ties evals and monitors. you can attach a prompt set for a route and get alerts if quality drops, and then the console surfaces failing traces and request logs for the examples.
03:36 Jordan Lee: latency vs cost 
 - can tracing itself add overhead?
03:40 Sara Patel: minimal; tracing is asynchronous and the payload is small. we have sampling controls so you can trace 1% or 100% of requests. full tracing at 100% may add a few ms of overhead on CPU-bound spans but it's usually negligible compared to model inference time.
03:56 Marcus Nguyen: curious about model rollbacks 
 - suppose a new model version causes more errors, how do we triage and rollback?
04:03 Sara Patel: console integrates with rollouts 
 - you can do canary at 5%, see errors and traces from the canary cohort, and auto-fallback to previous model if error rate exceeds threshold. we capture differences in tokenization and kernel selection which helps root cause.
04:18 Jordan Lee: nice. can we export traces to our internal tracing system?
04:22 Sara Patel: yes, we have exporters to popular tracing backends and you can forward request logs to S3 or BigQuery. we also support OpenTelemetry-compatible traces.
04:32 Alex Kim: question from earlier 
 - you mentioned dedicated vs hosted. what are you leaning towards for PoC?
04:38 Priya Rao: for PoC we want hosted for speed but with strong controls; long term probably Dedicated or Private for data residency.
04:46 Alex Kim: that's common. for hosted we can enable stricter network controls and RU-based access; for Private we can run in your VPC.
04:54 Jordan Lee: ok, let's walk a live debugging example 
 - we have a recent failing trace with hallucinations on a rerank route.
05:02 Sara Patel: great, show me the request id.
05:06 Jordan Lee: request id is req-20271111-44ab. (types)
05:12 Sara Patel: pulling it up 
 - i see the trace, the error is not a runtime crash but an unexpected token generation. pivoting to request logs 
 - prompt shows a user-injected system message that changed the context. there's also a model variant mismatch; the canary got the older vocab which caused tokenization issues.
05:34 Jordan Lee: aha, so tokenization mismatch 
 - where did that come from?
05:38 Sara Patel: looks like the rollout config updated model_alias but didn't pin tokenizer; we show that mapping in the rollout metadata and you can diff model versions in console.
05:50 Marcus Nguyen: can console detect regressions automatically?
05:54 Sara Patel: yes with Optimize you can set quality baselines and get alerts for regressions. also link failing prompts to traces so engineers can reproduce locally.
06:04 Jordan Lee: will you share a checklist for our engineering team to reproduce issues locally?
06:08 Sara Patel: absolutely, i'll drop a quickstart with examples and a local reproduce script.
06:14 Alex Kim: i want to highlight the request logs schema 
 - we include request_id, timestamp, route, model, model_version, latency_ms, token_count, status_code, error_class, user_metadata. we'll send a sample log file after the call.
06:28 Priya Rao: about throughput 
 - peak QPS for us will be around 120 rps with spikes to 300 for short windows. can Redwood handle that on hosted?
06:36 Sara Patel: yes on hosted we have autoscaling pools; for predictable latency at that scale we often recommend Dedicated with reserved capacity, but hosted can sustain bursts with burst capacity add-on. we can run a benchmark to show cost/latency tradeoffs.
06:50 Jordan Lee: benchmarks 
 - would like to see 95th latency numbers for our traffic profile.
06:54 Sara Patel: we'll run an internal bench with your sample traffic. please send seed traffic, prompt length distribution, and concurrency pattern.
07:04 Alex Kim: noted as an action item: Jordan to share sample traffic profile.
07:08 Jordan Lee: will do.
07:12 Marcus Nguyen: security follow-up 
 - do we get immutable audit logs for policy changes and who viewed traces?
07:18 Sara Patel: yes, we log admin actions and viewing of sensitive traces if you enable that setting; logs can be forwarded to your SIEM and we support time-limited console access.
07:30 Priya Rao: regulatory question 
 - HIPAA compliance posture?
07:34 Alex Kim: Redwood has an enterprise package for HIPAA-ready deployments; for PHI you'd want Private deployment and BAAs 
 - we'll include details in the security doc.
07:44 Jordan Lee: a couple small quibbles 
 - the UI sometimes abbreviates kernel names and the span labels can be cryptic. is there a glossary?
07:50 Sara Patel: yes glossary and span docs; we'll send those. also you can hover to expand labels in the UI. some auto transcription may read kernel as carnel in past exports, sorry for that.
08:02 Alex Kim: any other blockers on the compliance side?
08:06 Marcus Nguyen: need to review encryption in transit, key rotation policies, and how backups are handled.
08:12 Alex Kim: we'll include key rotation docs and backup retention notes in the packet.
08:18 Sara Patel: back to debugging flows 
 - here's a common pattern: error -> trace -> request log -> model diffs -> rollback. we demoed that flow. another is performance spike -> trace queue -> batchsize -> recommend config change.
08:36 Jordan Lee: can we simulate KV cache behavior in staging to validate improvements?
08:40 Sara Patel: yes, we can replay requests or run load tests; we also provide a simulation tool that estimates cache hit rates given prompt patterns.
08:50 Priya Rao: curious about cost visibility 
 - does the console show token-level cost per route?
08:54 Sara Patel: yes per-route token costs, and we have a cost explorer with breakdown by model, quantization, and route. you can set budgets and get alerts.
09:02 Jordan Lee: fine. quick question about log redaction 
 - is that applied before storage or available as a view filter?
09:08 Sara Patel: redaction happens at ingestion by default if configured; you can also do on-the-fly redaction for views but the raw encrypted logs remain with restricted access depending on your retention & encryption settings.
09:18 Alex Kim: wrapping up 
 - recap of next steps: send security docs, benchmark sheet, sample logs, schedule PoC check-in.
09:26 Priya Rao: thanks, that works.
09:30 Jordan Lee: appreciate it, looking forward to the sample log format.
09:34 Marcus Nguyen: thanks everyone.
09:36 Sara Patel: i'll follow up with links to SOC2, glossary, quickstart, and the reproduce script.
09:42 Alex Kim: meeting adjourned.
